clue.text: William or Kate Hardcastle

definitions.meaning: William I of England is known as William the ... after his Norman victory of 1066
the heroine of Goldsmith's comedy She Stoops to Conquer, who wins her suitor by posing as a barmaid

explanation.surface: A question about which of two figures, a king or a stage heroine, fits a description.
explanation.walkthrough: Both senses are allusions: William's epithet, and the title of the play Kate Hardcastle stars in, She Stoops to Conquer.
explanation.definitionFit: Each figure is a victor: one won a kingdom by battle, the other won a husband by stooping to trickery.

clue.text: Rising leader, beginning to train?

parts.note: a future officer still in training is a leader on the rise, starting out on instruction

explanation.surface: Describing an up-and-coming leader starting to learn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rising leader' suggests an ambitious politician; it is a young person training for military command.
explanation.definitionFit: A trainee at a military or police academy is a prospective officer.

clue.text: A case of insufficient evidence

parts.note: a case read as a lawsuit: a court dismisses a claim where the plaintiff fails to make out a case

explanation.surface: Describing a weak court case.
explanation.walkthrough: This legal term is the dismissal of a lawsuit because the plaintiff has not shown enough evidence.
explanation.definitionFit: In law, a judgment against a plaintiff who cannot prove a case stops the action.

clue.text: Unoccupied, so restless

explanation.surface: Someone with nothing to do and therefore fidgety.
explanation.definitionFit: The word describes land without colonists and a mind that is agitated or troubled.

clue.text: Verdicts on suit — loser ruined

indicators.note: ruined means wrecked, so the letters of the three words are broken up and rebuilt

explanation.surface: Court rulings on a lawsuit leave the losing party bankrupt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ruined' looks like the loser's fate; it shuffles ONSUITLOSER.
explanation.definitionFit: Formal decisions reached by a committee or court are its findings.

clue.text: Port drunk by Americans

definitions.meaning: A Cinque Port in East Sussex
the whiskey distilled from this grain is popular in the United States

explanation.surface: A fortified wine consumed by people from the US.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Port' suggests the drink; it is the harbour town in Sussex, one of England's historic Cinque Ports.
explanation.definitionFit: The name is both a Sussex harbour town and an American grain whiskey.

clue.text: His golden rule was impossible to live by

definitions.text: His golden rule was impossible to live by

parts.words: His golden rule was impossible to live by
parts.note: a golden rule usually means a guiding principle, but here it is the curse of the mythical king whose touch turned everything, even his food, to gold

explanation.surface: A remark about someone whose guiding principle proved impractical.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Golden rule' looks like a moral maxim; it is literally a reign of gold, and he could not live because his food became metal.
explanation.definitionFit: The Phrygian king of myth was granted a touch that made gold of all he handled, so he could not eat.

clue.text: Make fast time initially inside this vehicle

indicators.note: inside says the first letter goes within the word for make fast

parts.note: to moor a boat is to make it fast

indicators.note: initially picks the first letter of the word time

explanation.surface: Urging speed inside a car.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Make fast' looks like speed up; it means to tie up a boat, MOOR.
explanation.definitionFit: A car is commonly called this in British speech.

clue.text: Recite ingredients of medical concoction

indicators.note: a concoction is a mixture, so the letters of the word medical are mixed up as ingredients

explanation.surface: Reading out the list of components of a drug.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ingredients of' and 'concoction' together say the letters of MEDICAL are remixed.
explanation.definitionFit: To deliver a speech or poem in an oratorical way is to recite it.

clue.text: Those ranked with Troy in greatness, perhaps

definitions.text: Those ranked with Troy in greatness, perhaps

parts.words: Those ranked with Troy in greatness, perhaps
parts.note: Troy is not the ancient city but Sergeant Frank Troy of Hardy's Far from the Madding Crowd, so those of equal rank share his title

explanation.surface: Things considered equal to the ancient city of Troy in grandeur.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Troy' suggests the city of Homer; it is the dashing soldier Troy in Hardy's Far from the Madding Crowd.
explanation.definitionFit: Non-commissioned officers of the same grade as Hardy's soldier Troy.

clue.text: Hardy characters in soap opera?

parts.note: Thomas Hardy wrote an epic drama about Napoleonic rulers, and the American soap Dynasty was full of powerful ruling families

explanation.surface: A question about tough characters appearing in a television serial.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hardy' reads as tough, but it is the novelist Thomas Hardy, whose verse drama on the Napoleonic wars shares its title with the answer; the soap is Dynasty.
explanation.definitionFit: Members of ruling families or hereditary rulers, the people in Hardy's drama and in the soap Dynasty.

clue.text: Siren — one in centre going off

indicators.note: in says the letter for one goes into the word centre
going off means spoiling, like food, so the letters of the combined pieces are jumbled

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: A warning siren with one unit in the middle of town going off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Going off' suggests an alarm sounding; it is the anagram signal for I set in CENTRE.
explanation.definitionFit: A siren in myth lures sailors, so she is a temptress who draws people on.

clue.text: Guy in West End with relation

indicators.note: End here means the final letter of the word West, not the London district

parts.note: an aunt is a relation

explanation.surface: A man in London's West End with a relative.
explanation.walkthrough: 'West End' looks like the London theatre district; 'End' picks the last letter of West. 'Guy' is the verb, to mock.
explanation.definitionFit: To guy someone is to ridicule them, which is to jeer or mock.

clue.text: Letters from abroad, not USA, put in here

definitions.text: Letters from abroad, not USA, put in here

parts.words: Letters from abroad, not USA, put in here
parts.note: letters read as printing type: the small letters that are not capitals live in the bottom tray of a compositor's case, and 'abroad' read as the capitals' opposite

explanation.surface: A note about where mail from overseas, but not from America, is put.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Letters' suggests mail; in printing, small letters (not capitals) are kept in the bottom tray of the type case. 'Not USA' hints at the capitals USA, which belong in the upper case.
explanation.definitionFit: In hand typesetting the minuscule letters were kept in the bottom tray of type, so the tray gave its name to small letters.

clue.text: Don't pay novice to give this course

parts.note: to welsh is to fail to pay a debt
a rabbit is British slang for a poor player, a beginner

explanation.surface: Someone telling a beginner not to pay for something.
explanation.walkthrough: Rabbit is British slang for an inept player, notably at golf, cricket or tennis. The dish is cheese on toast.
explanation.definitionFit: The savoury cheese-on-toast dish is served as part of a meal.

clue.text: Save? On the contrary

definitions.meaning: save as a preposition means except
a conjunction introducing a contrast, as in however

explanation.surface: A one-word query followed by a contradiction.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both except (all save one) and however (introducing an objection).

clue.text: Not a choice state to be in

definitions.text: Not a choice state to be in

parts.words: Not a choice state to be in
parts.note: playing on the proverb that beggars can't be choosers: a choice state is not a pleasant one, and paupers have no choice

explanation.surface: A remark that some situation is unpleasant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not a choice state' reads as 'not a nice place', but alludes to the saying that beggars can't be choosers.
explanation.definitionFit: The condition of utter poverty, living as a mendicant, is a wretched way to live.

clue.text: March issue

parts.note: March reads as a month but is the family surname, and issue means offspring: the four March daughters

explanation.surface: Like the label on a magazine's spring edition.
explanation.walkthrough: 'March issue' suggests a magazine edition; it is the March sisters of Louisa May Alcott's novel, issue meaning children.
explanation.definitionFit: Alcott's novel follows Meg, Jo, Beth and Amy, the daughters of the March family.

clue.text: By no means appreciating what's despicable

definitions.meaning: read as two words: not gaining value

explanation.surface: Someone ungrateful described as contemptible.
explanation.walkthrough: Split it as WORTH LESS and it means falling in value, the opposite of appreciating.
explanation.definitionFit: Something of no merit or value is contemptible, and split in two the word means losing value.

clue.text: 21. perhaps? Surely she's older

parts.note: 21 refers to the prophet's name in 21 down, which was also borne by the American folk painter Grandma Moses, who began painting in her seventies

explanation.surface: Someone is guessed to be twenty-one, but must be older.
explanation.walkthrough: '21' looks like an age; it is a cross-reference to 21 down, the American folk painter Grandma Moses. The comma after 21 was misread as a full stop in this copy.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman with grandchildren is the mother of a parent, hence two generations older.

clue.text: Operation takes a long time for dogs' victim

parts.note: an act is a deed or operation
an eon is an age, a very long time

explanation.surface: A surgical procedure taking ages for an animal attacked by dogs.
explanation.walkthrough: In Greek myth the hunter Actaeon saw Artemis bathing, was turned into a stag and torn apart by his own hounds.
explanation.definitionFit: The mythical hunter was killed by his own hunting hounds.

clue.text: Transport Joan Hunter Dunn's admirer back

indicators.note: back says the word for the admirer is read backwards

parts.note: in John Betjeman's poem A Subaltern's Love-song, the speaker who adores Joan Hunter Dunn is a subaltern, a junior officer, shortened to sub

explanation.surface: Arranging travel home for an admirer of a woman.
explanation.walkthrough: Joan Hunter Dunn is the tennis-playing heroine of Betjeman's poem; her admirer is a subaltern, SUB.
explanation.definitionFit: A public road vehicle carrying passengers is a means of getting about.

clue.text: Fair lady left king's minstrel

parts.note: a fair-haired woman is a blonde

explanation.surface: A fair woman leaves the royal musician.
explanation.walkthrough: Legend says the troubadour Blondel found Richard the Lionheart imprisoned in Austria by singing a song they knew.
explanation.definitionFit: The troubadour of legend served Richard I of England.

clue.text: Bathing beauty 18 saw, one with a plant

parts.note: Actaeon, the answer to 18 down, saw the goddess Artemis bathing and was turned into a stag
one is the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: A hunter glimpsing a woman bathing, who is holding a plant.
explanation.walkthrough: 18 is a cross-reference to 18 down, Actaeon, whose glimpse of the bathing goddess cost him his life.
explanation.definitionFit: This genus includes wormwood and mugwort, aromatic herbs named after the Greek goddess.

clue.text: The prophet Amos, esteemed to some extent

indicators.note: to some extent says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A biblical prophet, Amos, held in some esteem.
explanation.walkthrough: Amos is itself a prophet, the decoy definition; the answer runs through aMOS ESteemed.
explanation.definitionFit: The Hebrew lawgiver who led Israel from Egypt is the great prophet of the Old Testament.

clue.text: How one has pointless fuss

indicators.note: pointless says the compass points, the letters for north, south, east and west, are removed from the phrase

explanation.surface: Asking how someone makes a fuss over nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pointless' looks like futile; it strips the compass points W, N, E and S from HOWONEHAS.
explanation.definitionFit: A commotion or noisy to-do is a fuss, British slang.

clue.text: Land role in Sheridan play

definitions.meaning: plots of ground measured in units
The cowardly country squire in Sheridan's comedy The Rivals

explanation.surface: Ground set aside for a part in an eighteenth-century comedy.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means landed estate and is the surname of a comic squire in The Rivals.

clue.text: Assistant in theatre of one sort or another

definitions.text: Assistant in theatre of one sort or another

parts.words: Assistant in theatre of one sort or another
parts.note: in a playhouse this helper looks after an actor's costumes, while in an operating theatre a nurse puts on wound bandages; a kitchen cupboard shares the name

explanation.surface: Describing a helper working in some kind of theatre.
explanation.walkthrough: Theatre can be a playhouse or an operating theatre: one helper looks after actors' costumes, the other applies dressings to wounds.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both a backstage costume assistant and a surgeon's helper who applies bandages.

clue.text: Wife and kid

definitions.meaning: Eve was made from Adam's ..., so a wife is jokingly called a man's ...

explanation.surface: A married couple's child.
explanation.definitionFit: A wife is humorously called a rib after Genesis, and to tease is to rib.

clue.text: Despicable sort…, this old-fashioned doctor?

definitions.meaning: British slang for a contemptible person
physicians once let blood from patients as a treatment

explanation.surface: Calling someone contemptible and suggesting he is an antique physician.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is British slang for a rotter, and also names a physician who let blood as a cure.

clue.text: They make a nice tub for West Country sailors

parts.note: Bath is a city in the West Country, south-west England
old salts are experienced sailors

explanation.surface: Something pleasant to bathe in for sailors from south-west England.
explanation.walkthrough: The West Country is south-west England; Bath is one of its cities.
